text: Your 2027 doesn't start on the first of January. In Vedic numerology, your personal year starts on your birthday.
And the number many calculators give you is worked out a different way. If a new year has ever felt like it never really started, you may have been reading the wrong year.
In this lesson you'll learn how your personal year is worked out, what each of the nine years is for, the mistakes to avoid, and how to find yours for 2027.
A personal year is one number that colours twelve months of your life. It runs from one birthday to the next, not from January to December.
It doesn't predict events. It tells you what a year is good for. When to start, when to build, when to slow down and think.
If you watched the first lesson, you already know your Moolank, the number from the day you were born. You'll need it here.
Your personal year comes from four numbers, added together.
One. The last two digits of the year. For 2027, that's twenty-seven.
Two. Your Moolank.
Three. Your birth month, brought down to one digit. October is ten, so it becomes one.
Four. The planet of the weekday your birthday falls on that year. This is the one almost everyone misses.
Sunday is the Sun, one. Monday, the Moon, two. Tuesday, Mars, nine. Wednesday, Mercury, five. Thursday, Jupiter, three. Friday, Venus, six. And Saturday, Saturn, eight.
Add the four numbers, then keep adding the digits until one digit is left. That's your personal year.
Let's take the example from the first lesson. Someone born on the fourteenth of August, nineteen ninety-six. Their Moolank is five.
In 2027, the fourteenth of August falls on a Saturday. And Saturday is Saturn. Number eight.
So it's twenty-seven, plus five, plus eight for August, plus eight for Saturday. That's forty-eight. Four plus eight is twelve. One plus two is three.
Their 2027 is a three. A Jupiter year, a year for growth and counsel. And it begins on the fourteenth of August 2027, not on New Year's Day.
Until then, they're still in their 2026 year. In 2026, their birthday fell on a Friday, Venus, six. Twenty-six plus five plus eight plus six is forty-five. Four plus five is nine. A Mars year.
Second example. Born on the twenty-ninth of March, nineteen ninety. Moolank two. March is three. In 2027, the twenty-ninth of March is a Monday, the Moon, two.
Twenty-seven plus two plus three plus two is thirty-four. Three plus four is seven. A Ketu year, a year for reflection, from the twenty-ninth of March.
Here's what each of the nine years is for.
One, the Sun. A year for beginning. Starting something of your own, and taking the decision you've been circling.
Two, the Moon. A year for partnership. Building alongside others, and trusting your intuition over a rigid plan.
Three, Jupiter. A year for growth and counsel. Learning, teaching, and speaking up clearly.
Four, Rahu. A year for careful groundwork. Research and planning, and a second opinion before big decisions.
Five, Mercury. A year for deals and connection. Negotiating, networking, and sharpening your money sense.
Six, Venus. A year for relationships and care. Close relationships, creative work, and looking after the people you love.
Seven, Ketu. A year for reflection. Deep study, inner work, rest, and trusting your intuition.
Eight, Saturn. A year for discipline. Finishing what you started, and long-term planning. It can feel slow, and it rewards patience.
Nine, Mars. A year for decisive action. Taking a stand, and pushing a project through to the end.
So why do people get their personal year wrong? Three reasons.
Mistake one. Starting it on the first of January. Your year turns on your birthday. If your birthday is in August, most of the calendar year still belongs to your last personal year.

Mistake two. Adding the day, the month and the new year. For the fourteenth of August that gives twenty-four, which is six. In this method it's a three. A different number, and a different kind of year.

Mistake three. Forgetting the weekday. It's why two people with the same Moolank and the same birth month can still be in different years. Your birthday moves through the week, and your year moves with it.
